title: Canadian Raising — about, out, house
focus: The raised diphthong before voiceless consonants
target_sentence: I'm out and about with my house key.
tip: Start the vowel higher and round it — say 'ab-OUT' with a quick, crisp finish. The raised sound is what makes 'about' sound unmistakably Canadian.

title: The sorry vowel — not sah-ree
tip: Round your lips like you're starting to say 'sore' — short and warm, never flat like 'sah'. It's the most useful vowel in Canada.

title: The eh? tag — rise, don't fall
focus: Rising pitch on the eh? tag
tip: End 'eh' with your voice going UP — it quietly asks 'right?' without saying the words. A falling eh? sounds like a statement, not a question.

title: The flapped T — water, better
focus: The quick d-like T between vowels
target_sentence: Could I get a water? That's better, thanks.
tip: When a T sits between two vowels, it becomes a light tap — like a quick 'd', never a hard 't'. Say 'wa-der', not 'wa-ter'.

title: Out and about — phrase rhythm
focus: Linking words into one smooth phrase
target_sentence: I've been out and about all morning.
tip: Let the words blur together — 'out-n-about'. Canadians don't stop between them, and the phrase sounds lazy but friendly.

title: Canadian uniform words — toque, runners, chesterfield
target_sentence: Grab your toque and runners, then sit on the chesterfield.
tip: Toque rhymes with 'duke' — no 'k' at the end. Runners are running shoes, and a chesterfield is just a couch. Say them with confidence.

title: Clear th in thanks and three
focus: The /θ/ sound — tongue between the teeth
target_sentence: Thanks — I'll see you at three.
tip: Touch your tongue lightly between your teeth and blow air through. No 't' or 's' substitutes — Canadians hear the difference instantly.

title: Casual -in' — goin', grabbin'
focus: The relaxed -ing ending in casual speech
target_sentence: I'm goin' out, grabbin' a coffee.
tip: In friendly chat the 'g' drops: 'goin', 'grabbin'. Keep it casual out loud, but never in formal writing.

title: Polite request melody — Could you just…?
focus: The rising, softened melody of a polite ask
target_sentence: Could you just send that over?
tip: The melody rises gently at the end — light, never commanding. 'Just' is a softener here, not an order.

title: Reductions — How's it goin'?
target_sentence: How's it goin'? Not bad, you?
tip: 'How's it' becomes one sound — 'ha-zi-go-in'. It's the most common greeting in Canada; own it.

title: Minimal pair — sorry vs sore-y
focus: Vowel length: sorry is short, sore-y is long
tip: Say 'sorry' in a hurry — one quick vowel. 'Sore-y' stretches it out. Length is the whole difference, and Canadians keep sorry quick.

title: Sentence stress — I'm just gonna grab a double-double
focus: Stressing the key words, gliding over the rest
target_sentence: I'm just gonna grab a double-double.
tip: Stress 'grab' and 'double-double'; glide over 'just gonna a'. It's a Canadian coffee order, said with rhythm and a smile.
